# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

Sample text:
---
# The Annotated

The box was heavier than it looked.

Hal Weatherby set it on the counter with a grunt that turned into an apology. "My mother's," he said, as if that explained the weight. "She passed in March. I've been going through things."

Elena looked at the box. It was a banker's box, the kind with a plastic handle and a lid that never quite fit right, and it had been taped shut at least twice. "Books?"

"Books." Hal pushed his glasses up his nose. "She was a reader. I'm not. I tried, but." He shrugged. "They're old. Some are library books, I think. I didn't know what to do with them, and someone said you buy used books, so."

Elena ran a used bookstore called The Second Shelf. It was a narrow shop wedged between a Thai restaurant and a vacuum repair place, and it smelled of paper and dust and the lemongrass that drifted through the wall. She bought books, yes, but she bought them the way a gardener buys compost — with an eye for what could be turned into something else.

"Let's see what we've got," she said, and cut the tape with a box cutter.

The first layer was unremarkable: a couple of paperback thrillers with cracked spines, a hardcover biography of someone Elena had never heard of, a cookbook with a butter stain on the cover. She set them aside. The second layer was older. Cloth-bound, mostly, with titles stamped in gold that had worn down to the ghost of gold. A poetry anthology. A history of the Ottoman Empire. A novel called *The Weather of Our Days*, which Elena had never seen before and which had a title page with no publisher's mark — privately printed, maybe.

And then, at the bottom, four books with the same stamp on the inside cover: a circle of oak leaves, and beneath it, PROPERTY OF THE FAIRMOUNT LIBRARY. Below the stamp, someone had written 1983 in pencil.

Fairmount Library had burned in 1985. Elena knew this the way she knew all the small tragedies of the town's book world — the way she knew that the shop three doors down had flooded in '92 and lost its entire science section, the way she knew that old Mrs. Petrakis had donated her late husband's collection with a note that said only, "He would have wanted them to be read." The Fairmount fire had been arson, or faulty wiring; the reports disagreed, and by now nobody cared. What mattered was that the library had never been rebuilt. The lot was a parking garage now.

Elena opened the first of the four. It was a novel — *The Door Between Worlds*, by someone named I. M. Sørensen — and the moment she fanned the pages, she saw the annotations.

Not standard annotations. Not underlines or brackets or the occasional *yes!* in the margin. These were letters.

*You were right about the third chapter*, said a line in pencil at the top of the first page. *It's all foreshadowing. The weather vane, the broken glass — it's all going to come back at the end. I won't spoil it. But I'm reading slower now, because I don't want to get there.*

Below it, in blue ink, in a different hand: *You're reading slower? I've been reading the same paragraph for three days. I keep going back. I keep thinking about what you said about the weather vane. I think you're right, but I also think it's a trap. Sørensen is too clever to give us a signal that simple.*

Elena turned the page. More.

*It's not a trap, it's a gift. She's a generous writer. The gift is that you can see it coming.*

*I don't know that I'd call it generous. I'd call it cruel. You and I both know what's going to happen to the weather vane.*

*We don't know that.*

*We don't.*

And so on, through the book. Two people, talking to each other through the margins of a library book that had been checked out in 1983 and never returned. Elena knew how this worked — she'd seen it before, in other books, the way readers who can't say things to each other's faces say them in the margins of something they both love. But she'd never seen it so sustained. Page after page, book after book. The pencil and the blue ink arguing, agreeing, joking, going quiet for a while and then picking up again a hundred pages later as if no time had passed.

She looked at the other three books. The pencil and the blue ink were in all of them. *The Door Between Worlds* — *A Field Guide to North American Mosses* — *Collected Poems of Anna Akhmatova* — *The Weather of Our Days*.

The last one was the same privately printed novel that had been in the box, the one without a publisher's mark. Elena opened it. The annotations started on the first page.

*You asked what I'm reading, and I'm embarrassed to tell you, because it's a novel by a person who doesn't exist. I made her up. I wrote this book myself, years ago, under a name I've never used before or since, and I printed forty copies at a print shop in Boston, and I've been watching them show up in used bookstores ever since. This is one of them. You are holding my book. I don't know why I'm telling you this. I think it's because I'm going to move away, and I think it's because you're the only person I've ever told. Read it slowly. There's no hurry. I'll be gone by the time you finish.*

Below that, in blue ink, a single sentence:

*I'll read it so slowly it will take me years. And when I finish, I'll find you.*

Elena read it twice. Then she called Hal Weatherby.

---

Hal brought his mother's address book. They sat in the back of The Second Shelf with the four library books and the privately printed novel and a pot of tea that went cold because neither of them drank it.

"My mother's name was Louise," he said. "Louise Weatherby. She never married. She lived in the same house her whole life, the one on Summit Street, and she worked at the post office for thirty-one years. And I never knew —" He stopped. "I never knew she did anything like this."

"She was a reader," Elena said.

"She was a reader," he agreed. "She read the cereal boxes. She read the labels on the canned beans. I don't know why I'm surprised."

The pencil hand — Louise — had gone by Louisa, she'd told him in the margins. *Louisa*, because it sounded like someone who wrote in margins. The blue ink had gone by Frank, or maybe it was a nickname for something else, but Frank was what appeared most often. Frank had written a novel under the name I. M. Sørensen and printed forty copies and moved away. The books had been due back at the Fairmount Library on a date that had come and gone in the spring of 1985, and then the library had burned, and there was no one left to return them to.

"He was in the hospital," Hal said. "In 1985. That's what Louise wrote, in another one, the one I didn't give you. She wrote it in the margins of a book she never checked out, a book she bought for a nickel at a garage sale, because she'd run out of library books and she still needed a place to write to him. *You're in the hospital, and I can't visit, and I don't know if you'll read this, but I'm writing it anyway.*" He took a breath. "He died. I looked it up. Frank Murphy, born 1941, died April 1985. Pneumonia. He was forty-four."

Elena thought about the sentence in blue ink, the last one, the one that was almost a promise.

*I'll read it so slowly it will take me years. And when I finish, I'll find you.*

He hadn't finished. He'd been reading the same paragraph for three days, and then he'd been in a hospital bed, and Louise had been writing to him in the margins of a garage-sale book, and the library had burned, and nobody had ever known.

"I'd like to buy them," Elena said.

Hal looked at her. "They're library books."

"The library is a parking garage."

"I know."

"I'll keep them together," she said. "I'll put them on the shelf, and I'll write a little card that says what they are, and if anyone ever wants to know, the card will tell them. Not who Frank and Louise were — I won't put that. But what the books are. A conversation in the margins."

Hal was quiet for a while. Then he said, "She would have liked that."

"How do you know?"

He shrugged. "She kept them. She kept them for forty years. She didn't return them when the library burned, she didn't throw them away, she didn't let me throw them away. She kept them in a box in her closet, and she must have known I'd find them, and she must have known I'd bring them to a bookstore, because she knew I didn't read, she knew I wouldn't know what to do. She knew." He stood up. "She wanted someone to read them. That's what she wanted."

Elena walked him to the door. The lemongrass from the restaurant next door was stronger now, and the light was doing that thing it did in late afternoon, going gold and horizontal, making the dust in the air stand out like something worth looking at.

"You don't have to sell me the books," she said. "You can keep them. They're yours."

Hal shook his head. "They're not mine. They're hers. And they're his." He stepped out onto the sidewalk. "Put them on the shelf."

---

The card Elena wrote said:

*Four books from the Fairmount Library, checked out in 1983 and never returned. The library burned in 1985. Inside, in pencil and blue ink, two people are talking to each other. One of them wrote one of these books. The other one was reading it. They never met in person. Read the margins.*

She put the books on the shelf near the front of the store, where the light was best, and she put the privately printed novel on top, with the first page open, so that anyone who picked it up would see what Louise had written there, and what Frank had written back.

*I'll read it so slowly it will take me years. And when I finish, I'll find you.*

Nobody ever asked about the books. That was the thing. In a used bookstore, you learn that most people don't ask about anything. But every so often, someone would pick up the novel, and they'd read the first page, and then they'd turn to the next page, and the next. And Elena would watch from behind the counter, and she'd think about the way a story can outlast the people who made it, and the way a conversation can go on for forty years, and the way a book, even a library book, even a book that's due back at a library that no longer exists, can be a place where someone is still waiting to be found.

She never took the card down. It's still there.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A literary short story built around a mystery in annotated books and a bittersweet reunion that never happens.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient and observant, letting small physical details—a box that “never quite fit right,” lemongrass through the shop wall, dust in late-afternoon light—carry emotional weight. Its pathos comes from the gap between an intimate correspondence preserved in books and the lives that ended before the writers could meet. The story invites the reader to treat reading as a form of companionship and preservation, and to notice how ordinary objects can hold a private history.

## What the model chose to foreground
It foregrounds books not just as treasured objects but as places where people can speak across distance and time. The central moral emphasis is on keeping a conversation available to others without claiming ownership of its secrets: Elena displays the books, but withholds Frank and Louise’s names. The mood is tender and elegiac, softened by practical kindness and the possibility that someone else might read the margins.

## Evidence line
> She bought books, yes, but she bought them the way a gardener buys compost — with an eye for what could be turned into something else.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The story coherently returns to books as vessels of connection and memory, with a distinctive, restrained tenderness shaping both its details and resolution.
